clue.text: Poe as reformed fabulist

indicators.note: reformed means made over into a new shape, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Edgar Allan Poe turns over a new leaf and becomes a teller of fables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges POEAS, the letters of 'Poe as'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek slave credited with the classic animal fables is the archetypal fabulist.

clue.text: Hair on account for women players

parts.note: tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: A bill for hairdressing charged to the female members of the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts TRESSES below AC.
explanation.definitionFit: Female performers on stage or screen are the women who play roles.

clue.text: Christine 1902-83 (wrong dates)

indicators.note: the dates are said to be wrong, so their letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A biographical entry whose birth and death years have been printed incorrectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges DATES. The Australian novelist (The Man Who Loved Children) lived 1902 to 1983; the clue as printed gives her first name as Christine, where she is usually Christina.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist named by the dates is the Australian writer Christina, author of The Man Who Loved Children.

clue.text: Father of the French livre, and fellow humourist

parts.note: père is French for father
the livre was an old French pound, and L is the abbreviation for a pound
man means fellow, chap

explanation.surface: Someone invents the French currency and is also a comic writer.
explanation.walkthrough: S. J. Perelman was an American humorous writer for The New Yorker.
explanation.definitionFit: S. J. Perelman was an American comic writer of New Yorker pieces and Marx Brothers scripts.

clue.text: Daydreamer like Swithin St Cleeve

definitions.meaning: someone with head in the clouds, an idle dreamer
Swithin St Cleeve is the young astronomer of Hardy's Two on a Tower

explanation.surface: A dreamy fellow resembling Hardy's young hero.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamer gazes idly at the sky, as Hardy's astronomer hero literally watches the heavens.

clue.text: Miss Gibbons's farmer's boy starts some exceptionally trite homily

indicators.note: the starts of the next four words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: A farm lad from a novel begins a dull sermon.
explanation.walkthrough: Stella Gibbons wrote Cold Comfort Farm, where Seth Starkadder is the farmer's handsome son.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cold Comfort Farm the brooding son of the Starkadder household bears this name.

clue.text: Ace adlib is taken wrongly in Otway piece

indicators.note: taken wrongly means misread, so these letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: An actor's improvised line is misunderstood during a Restoration play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken wrongly' rearranges ACEADLIBIS. Thomas Otway was a Restoration dramatist whose first tragedy (1675) is named after the Athenian general.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Otway's first tragedy, of 1675, takes its title from the Athenian statesman and general.

clue.text: Some influence of quango dwindling rapidly for husband of early feminist

indicators.note: some of the following words means a run of their letters is taken

explanation.surface: A government body's sway fades fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks letters out of 'quango dwindling'. William Godwin married Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The philosopher William married Mary Wollstonecraft, the pioneering feminist writer.

clue.text: Spirit of the times is about size, get it?

indicators.note: about here means turned around and rearranged, so the following letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A punning question about the mood of the age being a matter of scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SIZEGETIT, the letters of 'size, get it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The German compound means the prevailing mood or outlook of an era.

clue.text: Manages to include English in early riddles

indicators.note: one word is made to include another, so the second goes inside the first

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it

explanation.surface: Someone contrives to put English into ancient puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Germanic letters carved as charms, and in old usage a rune was a secret or mystery.

clue.text: Reviewer suggests play based on the

indicators.note: one part is built on another, so the reviewer word follows the word given as it is

parts.note: taken as written
a critic reviews books or plays

explanation.surface: A reviewer hints that a drama has been adapted from a single article.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheridan's comedy The Critic (1779) satirises theatre reviewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's 1779 farce mocking reviewers and the theatre world carries this title.

clue.text: Reportedly (and in fact) spirits

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so the word for spirits is spoken

parts.note: gin is a spirit drink

explanation.surface: Spirits are said to be spirits, and truly are.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for alcoholic spirit (GIN) is said aloud, and the result also names supernatural spirits of Arabian lore.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islamic and Arabian legend these are supernatural beings, genies.

clue.text: What Macbeth hoped his blow might be

definitions.text: What Macbeth hoped his blow might be

parts.words: What Macbeth hoped his blow might be
parts.note: Macbeth hopes that the dagger stroke against Duncan might be 'the be-all and the' final settlement of everything

explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's soliloquy wishes the murder could be the be-all and the final conclusion of the matter.

clue.text: Condenses a former laureate

parts.note: Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate from 1913 to 1930

explanation.surface: A past Poet Laureate is accused of cutting things short.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten or condense it.

clue.text: Some of his characters seem to have found him elusive

definitions.text: Some of his characters seem to have found him elusive

parts.words: Some of his characters seem to have found him elusive
parts.note: refers to the Italian dramatist's play Six Characters in Search of an Author, whose characters hunt for their writer

explanation.definitionFit: The Italian playwright wrote Six Characters in Search of an Author, about figures seeking their creator.

clue.text: Cabal's a bit put out in period of rest

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A secret clique is annoyed during its time off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' rearranges CABALSABIT; the possessive apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A leave of absence, traditionally for academics, granted for rest or study.

clue.text: Novelist of the West Country increasingly macabre? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: the two words of the phrase are to be put the other way round, so the macabre word comes first

parts.note: black, as in black humour, means macabre
more means increasingly, as in more and more

explanation.surface: Is a regional novelist getting gloomier? On the contrary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'increasingly macabre' gives MORE BLACK; 'Quite the reverse' swaps their order. R. D. Blackmore wrote Lorna Doone, set on Exmoor in the West Country of England.
explanation.definitionFit: R. D. Blackmore set his romance Lorna Doone on Exmoor in south-west England.

clue.text: Rail return for Billy

indicators.note: a return journey goes back the way it came, so the word rail is read backwards

explanation.surface: Buying a return train ticket for a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns RAIL backwards. Billy Liar is Keith Waterhouse's novel about a fantasising young clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Waterhouse's daydreaming hero is named Billy, with this word as his surname.

clue.text: Where Beecham let the orchestra "play as they like "

definitions.text: Where Beecham let the orchestra "play as they like

parts.words: Where Beecham let the orchestra "play as they like "
parts.note: the conductor Sir Thomas Beecham let players do as they pleased in practice sessions before a concert

explanation.definitionFit: A practice run before a performance, where Beecham famously let the players have their head.

clue.text: Some harmless birds associated with aggressive women by Ransome

definitions.meaning: small migrating birds with forked tails

definitions.text: associated with aggressive women by Ransome
definitions.meaning: Arthur Ransome's children's novel pairs this word with Amazons, the warrior women of legend

explanation.surface: Gentle birds kept company with fierce women in a children's author's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome's Swallows and Amazons pairs the birds with the warrior women of Greek myth.

clue.text: Closure for Basil

definitions.meaning: a fastening or stopper that shuts something tight
Basil is the Christian name of the rogue in Evelyn Waugh's novels such as Put Out More Flags

explanation.surface: A herb is being used to shut something.
explanation.definitionFit: A stamp that closes a document or joint; and Waugh's scapegrace Basil bears this surname.

clue.text: Diviner Cooper naval tale

definitions.meaning: a dowser who finds underground springs with a forked stick
James Fenimore Cooper wrote a sea novel of this title in 1830

explanation.surface: A clairvoyant tells a story of the navy by an American novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowser seeking springs; also the title of James Fenimore Cooper's 1830 nautical romance.

clue.text: Part of poet booked by Burgess

definitions.text: Part of poet booked by Burgess

parts.words: Part of poet booked by Burgess
parts.note: Anthony Burgess wrote a novel about the interior of the poet Enderby, Mr Enderby's innards

explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Burgess titled a novel Inside Mr Enderby, about the poet of that name.

clue.text: Paul Goodman's managing in a novel way

definitions.meaning: the American writer Paul Goodman published a novel with this title in 1963
coping or getting by with what is available

explanation.surface: An American author's novel approach to running things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a novel way' tells you the second sense is the title of a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To get by with scant resources; also the title of Paul Goodman's 1963 novel.

clue.text: My French space traveller is an impressionist

parts.note: mon is French for my
ET is the alien from the film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial

explanation.surface: A Frenchman claims an alien visitor as a mimic of his own.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude, the French painter of water lilies, was a founder of the Impressionist movement.

clue.text: Unusual tongue results in defeat in Georgia

indicators.note: one thing is placed in another, so the defeat word sits inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
a loss is a defeat

explanation.surface: A strange language leads to a beating in the Deep South.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare anatomical word for the tongue, from the Greek.

clue.text: A London investment associated with James

definitions.text: A London investment associated with James

parts.words: A London investment associated with James
parts.note: investment is the military sense of besieging a place; Henry James wrote a story about the capital's high society on this theme

explanation.definitionFit: Investment means encircling a town in war; Henry James wrote The Siege of London.

clue.text: Hamlet referred to a divinity that shapes ours

definitions.text: Hamlet referred to a divinity that shapes ours

parts.words: Hamlet referred to a divinity that shapes ours
parts.note: quotes Hamlet's line about a divinity shaping our purposes or destinies, rough-hew them how we will

explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet says a divinity shapes our final aims or destinies, rough-hew them how we will.

clue.text: Not a ruthless mother-in-law

parts.note: the Old Testament matriarch is far from cruel and is literally not without Ruth, her devoted daughter-in-law

explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Ruth, Ruth stays loyal to her husband's mother, who is kind rather than cruel.

clue.text: Some capital characters of Maureen Duffy

definitions.meaning: people who live in the English capital city
Maureen Duffy published a novel with this title in 1983

explanation.surface: Excellent figures in a British novelist's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of the British capital; also Maureen Duffy's 1983 novel of city life.

clue.text: And some splendid chaps of Charles Kingsley

definitions.meaning: Charles Kingsley retold Greek myths for children under this title in 1856

explanation.surface: A few fine fellows from a Victorian clergyman's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave champions; also Charles Kingsley's 1856 book of Greek myths for children.

clue.text: She showed promise in 1977 but came full circle in 1984 before making changes in 1987

definitions.text: She showed promise in 1977 but came full circle in 1984 before making changes in 1987

parts.words: She showed promise in 1977 but came full circle in 1984 before making changes in 1987
parts.note: the dates and phrases point to the popular American novelist Danielle, whose titles include The Promise, Full Circle and Changes

explanation.definitionFit: Danielle, the American bestselling novelist, wrote The Promise, Full Circle and Changes.
